points.t: Sharp, salmon-pink plaques with silvery scale on elbows, knees, scalp and lower back. Check the nails.
IL-23/Th17/IL-17 inflammation speeds skin turnover to 3–5 days (normally about 28).
Emollient plus potent steroid and vitamin D analogue, with planned steroid breaks.
Erythroderma or generalised pustular psoriasis (same day). Joint symptoms: think psoriatic arthritis.

cause.lead: An immune loop that makes skin cells grow far too fast.
points: **Genes + trigger**: e.g. HLA-C*06:02; about a third have a family history.
**IL-23 → Th17 → IL-17** (plus TNF-α) drives inflammation.
Keratinocytes turn over in **3–5 days** instead of about 28 → thick, scaly plaques.
**Triggers**: strep throat (guttate), trauma (**Koebner**), drugs, smoking, alcohol, obesity, stress, HIV.

visuals.caption: Normal skin (left) vs psoriatic plaque (right): thick epidermis, long rete ridges, heaped scale, dilated capillaries and immune cells.
visuals.alt: Cross-section comparing normal skin with a thickened psoriatic plaque

features.lead: Well-defined, symmetrical, scaly plaques on extensor sites.
points: **Sharp edge**: salmon-pink plaques with silvery-white scale (contrast: ill-defined eczema).
**Auspitz sign**: pinpoint bleeding when scale is lifted.
**Sites**: elbows, knees, lower back, scalp (often past the hairline), natal cleft.
**Nails**: pitting, onycholysis, oil-drop patches. A clue to psoriatic arthritis risk.
**Skin of colour**: violaceous or grey plaques; marked, lasting pigment change.

visuals.caption: Where to look: front of the knees and hairline (left); points of the elbows, scalp, sacrum and natal cleft (right).
visuals.alt: Front and back body outlines with psoriasis plaques on knees, elbows, scalp and lower back

items.name: Chronic plaque
items.t: Thick silvery scale; about 80–90% of cases.

items.name: Guttate
items.t: Many small ‘raindrop’ plaques 2–3 weeks after strep throat.

items.name: Flexural (inverse)
items.t: Shiny, moist, little or no scale; no satellites.

items.name: Scalp
items.t: Thick adherent scale, beyond the hairline.

items.name: Palmoplantar
items.t: Sharp red scaly plaques or thick keratoderma with painful fissures.

points: Triggers: strep throat, skin trauma (Koebner), stress, smoking, alcohol, obesity.
**Drugs**: β-blockers, lithium, antimalarials, interferons, rapid steroid taper.
Family history (about a third); joint pain or swelling.
Morphology and distribution, **nails** and **joints**.
High-impact sites: face, hands, genitals, scalp.
Body surface area (BSA) and quality of life.
BSA over 10% or major impact: refer (Step 5).
Usually **none**: it is a clinical diagnosis.
Biopsy if unsure; throat swab after sore throat (guttate).
Screen **PEST** every year; CV risk (NICE).

cards.name: Seborrhoeic dermatitis
cards.clue: Greasier scale on the central face; can overlap (‘sebopsoriasis’).

cards.name: Candidal intertrigo
cards.clue: Satellite papules and pustules, macerated (flexural psoriasis has none).

cards.name: Lichen planus
cards.clue: Violaceous flat-topped papules, Wickham striae; wrists, mucosa.

cards.name: Pityriasis rosea
cards.clue: Herald patch, collarette scale, ‘Christmas-tree’ back (vs guttate).

cards.name: Discoid eczema
cards.clue: Coin-shaped, very itchy, often on the legs.

manage.lead: Aligned with NICE CG153 and CKS. Adults, trunk and limbs.

points: Emollients regularly: less scale and itch.
Weight, smoking, alcohol, stress support.
Report new joint pain or swelling.

rx.note: Plus a vitamin D analogue at a different time of day.
Or potent steroid BD short course, or coal tar.

points: Phototherapy; methotrexate, ciclosporin, acitretin.
Biologics or TYK2 inhibitors under NICE TAs. Not IP-initiated.

limits.t: Plan a 4-week break between potent courses.
Withdrawal can trigger rebound or pustular flares.

sites.t: Potent steroid lotion, gel or shampoo first; then combination or vitamin D. Salicylic acid for thick scale.
Mild–moderate steroid, max 2 weeks. Never potent here. Calcineurin inhibitor (specialist-led) if needed.
Keratolytics, potent/very potent steroid ± calcipotriol, overnight occlusion. Refer early.
NICE: refer to a specialist at presentation.
Do not stop a β-blocker alone: discuss with GP or cardiology.

items.t: Suspected **psoriatic arthritis**: swollen or painful joints, dactylitis, enthesitis → rheumatology.
BSA over 10%, moderate or worse, topical failure or big quality-of-life impact → phototherapy or systemics.
Severe nail disease, children, diagnostic doubt.

pearls.t: Psoriasis is **chronic**; treatment is intermittent and relapse is expected.
Show how to apply. Gels and foams beat ointments for daytime adherence.
Spell out **steroid breaks** to prevent atrophy and rebound.
Calcipotriol/betamethasone brands vary by formulary: check locally.
Counsel on vaccines and infection risk before any immunosuppression.
Severe psoriasis carries a higher VTE and CV risk.

quiz.q: What happens to keratinocyte turnover in a psoriatic plaque?
quiz.a: It speeds up to 3–5 days instead of about 28, driven by IL-23/Th17/IL-17.

quiz.q: First-line topical plan for trunk and limbs in adults?
quiz.a: Potent steroid once daily plus a vitamin D analogue once daily (different times) for up to 4 weeks, with emollients.

quiz.q: Which steroid potency is safe for face, flexures and genitals?
quiz.a: Mild to moderate only, for up to 2 weeks. Never potent or very potent.
Erythroderma (over 90% of skin) and generalised pustular psoriasis.

quiz.q: Name three drugs that can trigger or worsen psoriasis.
quiz.a: β-blockers, lithium, antimalarials (also interferons and rapid steroid withdrawal).
